Page 3

Warmup: Concentration Problem

We start with a picture, keeping track of amount and volume.

Diagram description: Two tanks (Tank A and Tank B) are connected by pipes. Tank A has an inflow rate of 4 gal/min and Tank B has an inflow of 2 gal/min of water. Salt solution flows between the tanks at 5 g/min. Initial amounts: Tank A has 50 g of salt, Tank B has approximately 39 g. Flow rates are balanced so volumes remain constant at 94 gal and 24 gal respectively.

Setup: Two interconnected tanks with salt solution. Flow rates are balanced so each tank’s volume remains constant over time.

Relevant flow rates: 4 gal/min in, 5 g/min between tanks, 2 gal/min water inflow.

Observe: Volumes stay the same — the flow in equals the flow out for each tank.

Page 4

Setting Up the System of ODEs

We write the rate of change of salt in each tank using:

Rate of Change = Flow In − Flow Out

\[\frac{d(\text{amount})}{dt} = (\text{flow in}) - (\text{flow out})\]

For Tank 1, considering concentration \(\frac{x}{V_1}\) (amount divided by volume) and the relevant flow rates:

\[\dot{x} = (3)(4) + \cdots - \frac{x}{V_1}\cdot(\text{outflow rate})\]

Flow out from Tank 1 is the concentration in Tank 1 multiplied by the volumetric flow rate leaving. Similarly for Tank 2:

\[\dot{x} = \left(\frac{5}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot(\text{concentration in}) - \left(\text{flow out from Tank 1}\right)\]

Page 5

The System of ODEs

After setting up rates for both tanks, we arrive at a coupled system with initial conditions:

\[\begin{cases} \dot{x} = \cdots \\ \dot{y} = -\dfrac{x}{\;?\;} + \cdots + 25 \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = 50,\quad y(0) = 80\]

Key Insight: This says — if you know your current values of \(x\) and \(y\), you know how you are changing. That is, the derivatives \(\dot{x}\) and \(\dot{y}\) are completely determined by the current state \((x,\, y)\).

This is the fundamental property of a first-order autonomous system: the rate of change depends only on the current state, not on time directly.

Page 6

Observations from the System

Observation: Initially, the amount in Tank A will increase and in Tank B will decrease, based on the signs of \(\dot{x}\) and \(\dot{y}\) at the initial state.

Examining the vector field, the system appears to flow toward the point \((80,\, 70)\) in the \(xy\)-plane. Trajectories in the vicinity converge toward this point.

The point \((80,\, 70)\) appears to be a stable equilibrium — a state where \(\dot{x} = 0\) and \(\dot{y} = 0\) simultaneously, and nearby solutions approach it.

Page 7

Phase Plane: Direction Field and Solution Curves

Diagram description: A direction field (vector field) is plotted in the \(xy\)-plane with both axes ranging from approximately 5 to 95. Each lattice point has a small arrow indicating the local direction of the solution. Several colored solution curves are shown (purple, blue, cyan, green), originating from different initial conditions. All curves curve and converge toward the equilibrium point near \((80,\, 70)\). In the upper-left region arrows point right and down; in the lower-right they point left and up, consistent with a stable equilibrium attracting all nearby trajectories.

This phase portrait confirms the earlier observation: regardless of initial condition (within a neighborhood), all trajectories converge toward the equilibrium at approximately \((80,\, 70)\).

Page 8

Vector Fields

Definition: A vector field on the plane is a rule that assigns a vector to each point. For a two-dimensional system it takes the form:

\[\mathbf{F}(x,\, y,\, t) = \begin{pmatrix} f(x,\, y,\, t) \\ g(x,\, y,\, t) \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{(column notation)}\]

equivalently written in row notation as \(\bigl[f(x,y,t),\; g(x,y,t)\bigr]\).

Both notations represent the same object. Column notation is standard in linear algebra; row notation is used for compactness. The two components correspond to the right-hand sides of the two ODEs in the system.

Page 9

Autonomous Systems and Equilibria

The system can be written in vector form as:

\[\dot{\mathbf{c}} = \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix}\]

Definition (Autonomous): If time \(t\) does not appear explicitly in the vector field \(\mathbf{F}\), the system is called autonomous.

Example: The mixing tank problem with balanced volumes is autonomous — the ODEs depend only on \(x\) and \(y\), not on \(t\) directly.

Definition (Equilibrium): When \(\mathbf{F}(x,\, y) = \mathbf{0}\), the point \((x,\, y)\) is called an equilibrium (or equilibrium point) of the system.

At an equilibrium, both rates of change are zero simultaneously, so the solution remains stationary.

Page 10

Types of Equilibria

Diagram description: Three small phase portrait sketches are shown side by side. (1) Stable Equilibrium: arrows spiral or flow inward toward the equilibrium point. (2) Unstable Equilibrium: arrows flow outward away from the point. (3) Saddle (Neither): arrows flow inward along one axis and outward along the other, forming an X-shaped or hyperbolic pattern.

Stable Equilibrium: Nearby solutions approach the equilibrium as \(t \to \infty\). (Arrows point inward.)

Unstable Equilibrium: Nearby solutions move away from the equilibrium as \(t \to \infty\). (Arrows point outward.)

Saddle (Neither): Some nearby solutions approach and others move away, depending on direction. This is called a saddle point.

Page 11

System IVPs (Initial Value Problems)

Setup: Given a system of first-order ODEs

\[\dot{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Y},\, t)\]

and an initial condition \(\mathbf{Y}(0) = \mathbf{Y}_0\), we can sketch solution curves by following the direction vectors of the field \(\mathbf{F}\).

The idea is analogous to the single-variable case: at each point \((x,\, y)\), the vector field gives the instantaneous direction of motion. Starting from the initial point, tracing the arrows step-by-step yields an approximate solution curve.

Page 12

Exercise: Sketching a Solution Curve (Unstable Spiral)

Sketch an approximate solution to the system with the given initial value:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 0.5x - 1y + 0 \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1x + 0.5y + 0 \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = 0,\quad y(0) = 0\]
Diagram description: A vector field on a grid with both axes from \(-4\) to \(4\). Blue arrows at each grid point show the direction \((dx/dt,\, dy/dt)\). The arrows rotate counterclockwise and point outward, indicating an unstable spiral centered at the origin. Starting from \((0,0)\) — which is the equilibrium — the solution is the constant \(x(t)=0,\; y(t)=0\) for all \(t\).

Because the initial condition \((0,\, 0)\) is the equilibrium of this system, the solution is the trivial constant solution \(x(t) = 0,\; y(t) = 0\) for all \(t\).

Page 13

Exercise: Sketching a Solution Curve (Stable Spiral)

Sketch an approximate solution to the system with the given initial value:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -0.5x - 1y + 0 \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1x - 0.5y + 0 \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = 3,\quad y(0) = 2\]
Diagram description: A vector field on a grid with both axes from \(-4\) to \(4\). The blue arrows indicate a clockwise rotation with inward spiraling, consistent with a stable spiral equilibrium at the origin. Starting from \((3,\, 2)\), the solution curve spirals inward, converging to the origin as \(t \to \infty\).

Unlike the previous example, the negative real part of the eigenvalues (\(-0.5\)) causes solutions to spiral inward toward the equilibrium at the origin. The nonzero imaginary part of the eigenvalues produces the rotational (spiraling) behavior.
